sections.title: Description
sections.summary: Vertical drains with preloading, used since the 1920s, shorten the drainage path while fill loads the soil. PVDs ('wick drains') are band-shaped geotextile-jacketed plastic cores, typically 4 in. wide by 1/8 to 3/8 in. thick; preload brings the site to grade, surcharge is extra fill later removed (Figure 2-1). Vacuum preloading is not covered.
sections.body: Consolidation of soft ground by vertical drains and preloading has been used since the 1920s: drains shorten the path for water to leave the soil while fill preloads it. Sand drains came first, then cardboard drains, then geotextile-encased prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs), now the most common; 'wick drain' is common in the U.S. but PVD is more apt since drainage is by pressure, not wicking. PVDs accelerate consolidation of soft saturated compressible soils under load. They are band shaped (rectangular) products of a geotextile jacket around a plastic core with channels, typically 4 inches wide by 1/8 to 3/8 inches thick (also called drainage wicks, band drains, strip drains). Aggregate columns (Chapter 5) and geotextile encased columns also drain vertically under similar principles, but PVD cost advantages have made them almost exclusive (exceptions in Section 2.4). The commonest transportation use is accelerating consolidation under bridge approach and other embankments on soft soils (Figure 2-1). Preload is load applied to induce settlement and consolidation, often the fill needed to reach final grade including the extra for settlement; surcharge is fill above final grade to accelerate settlement and/or minimize secondary consolidation, removed afterward. Vacuum preloading (one atmosphere applied through sealed soil, with PVDs) has seen little U.S. use and is not discussed further. (pp. 2-1 to 2-2)

sections.title: Historical Overview
sections.summary: Sand drains (U.S. patent 1926) dominated U.S. highway work until the early 1980s; Kjellman's cardboard wick (late 1930s), Wager's Geodrain (1972) and the Castleboard Drain led to PVDs, used in the U.S. since the mid-to-late 1970s. Corrugated-core PVDs now hold nearly 100% of the U.S. market; earthquake drains are 3 to 6 in. perforated pipes.
sections.body: A U.S. patent for a sand drain system was granted in 1926 (D. J. Moran); the California Division of Highways tested sand drains from 1933, and they were used almost exclusively for U.S. highway projects until the early 1980s. In Sweden Walter Kjellman developed the first PVD in the late 1930s, a three-layer cardboard 'Cardboard Wick' 4 inches by 1/8 inch, used after 1939; Sweden later reverted to sand drains. Oleg Wager patented the Geodrain in 1972 (plastic core with 27 grooved channels, paper filter); the Castleboard Drain in Japan used a geotextile filter. PVDs reached the U.S. in the mid-to-late 1970s; with Alidrain, acceptance grew rapidly and PVDs are now used almost exclusively for vertical drainage, on hundreds of projects yearly. Over 50 PVD types have been used worldwide, at least 10 in the U.S., mostly of two designs with an independent geotextile filter: corrugated core (straight channels, nearly 100 percent of the U.S. market) and studded core (more turbulent flow, slightly thicker, small market share for cost); no project data show either core better. Earthquake (EQ) drains, 3 to 6 inch corrugated perforated pipe wrapped in geotextile, have been introduced to mitigate liquefaction (Rollins et al. 2004; Rollins and Strand 2007) (Figure 2-2). (pp. 2-3 to 2-5)
key_points: Sand drains dominated U.S. highways until the early 1980s
Corrugated-core PVDs hold nearly 100% of the U.S. market; no data favor either core

sections.title: Focus and Scope
sections.summary: The chapter covers applications, feasibility, construction and monitoring, design, specifications and case histories. Main use: consolidating soft soils by preloading and/or surcharging; PVDs cut settlement time, the surcharge needed, and the time to gain strength where stability matters.
sections.body: The chapter acquaints the reader with vertical drain methods, drawing on practice and the primary references (Section 1.5). It covers applications, feasibility, construction procedures and monitoring, design concepts, specifications and case histories. The major use is consolidation of soft soils by preloading and/or surcharging; others are pressure relief wells against seepage pore pressures, lowering perched water tables, and reducing liquefaction potential. With surcharge or preload, PVDs (1) decrease the settlement time so construction finishes in reasonable time with minimal post-construction settlement, (2) decrease the surcharge or preload needed for a settlement in a given time, and (3) increase the rate of strength gain where stability is a concern; any one or a combination may justify them. (p. 2-6)
key_points: Main use: consolidation of soft soils by preloading and/or surcharging
Benefits: less time, less surcharge, faster strength gain

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: Glossary: consolidation, earthquake drains, geosynthetic, geotextile, preconsolidation stress, prefabricated vertical drain, preloading, primary consolidation, secondary compression, surcharge, wick drain.
sections.body: Consolidation: time-dependent settlement of saturated low-permeability fine-grained soil. Earthquake drains: high flow capacity synthetic vertical drains, 3 to 6 inch corrugated plastic pipe wrapped in geotextile, installed with a vibrating mandrel. Geosynthetic: planar polymeric product used with soil or rock as part of a project. Geotextile: permeable textile geosynthetic used as separator, filter or for stabilization. Preconsolidation stress: maximum past effective overburden stress. Prefabricated vertical drain (PVD): band shaped product of geotextile jacket around a channeled plastic core; water flows through the filter into the core and up and/or down to the nearest free draining layer. Preloading: load applied to induce settlement or consolidation, permanent or temporary. Primary consolidation: compression while excess pore pressures dissipate. Secondary compression: settlement at constant effective stress. Surcharge: extra load above the preload to accelerate consolidation or minimize secondary compression. Wick drain: another name for PVD. (pp. 2-6 to 2-7)
key_points: Preload vs surcharge; primary consolidation vs secondary compression
Wick drain is another name for PVD

sections.title: Preloading of Soft Soils
sections.summary: PVDs suit moderately to highly compressible, low-permeability, fully saturated soils, normally to slightly overconsolidated (or underconsolidated in reclamation), loaded beyond the preconsolidation stress; not usually highly organic soils or where secondary consolidation governs. Table 2-1 lists common transportation uses.
sections.body: PVDs are most commonly used where the soil is moderately to highly compressible, of low permeability and fully saturated: silts, clays, organic silts and clays, muck, peat, swamps, muskeg, sludge. Soils must be saturated and normally to slightly overconsolidated before loading; PVDs are also used in underconsolidated soils in land reclamation. Loading should exceed the preconsolidation stress for PVDs to be totally effective. Ordinarily PVDs are not used in highly organic materials or where secondary consolidation would cause significant post-construction settlement, though extra surcharge can reduce that effect. Table 2-1 (increase stability / accelerate settlements): highway roadway embankments yes/yes; highway structure approach fills yes/yes; airfield runways and taxiways yes/yes; earth embankment dams yes/yes; storage tanks yes/yes; pile foundations to reduce 'negative' skin friction no/yes; liquefaction mitigation yes/yes; land reclamation yes/yes. (p. 2-9)

sections.title: Special Application, Liquefaction Reduction
sections.summary: An emerging use: EQ drains (3 to 6 in. slotted pipes of high flow capacity) let seismic excess pore pressures in saturated granular soils dissipate, replacing gravel drains; limited research suggests some improvement (Rollins et al. 2004; Rollins and Strand 2007).
sections.body: An emerging use is drains to reduce liquefaction potential of saturated granular soils: they let excess pore pressures from seismic excitation dissipate rapidly, replacing the gravel drains used for about 30 years. These are EQ Drains, vertical slotted plastic pipes 3 to 6 inches in diameter with high flow capacity. Limited research has been done on the extent of liquefaction reduction, but some improvement appears likely (Rollins et al. 2004; Rollins and Strand 2007). (pp. 2-9 to 2-10)

sections.summary: Production averages 15,000 to 20,000 lineal feet per day per rig (two to three times that has been achieved); 15,000 ft per day is used for planning.

sections.title: Continuity of Drain
sections.summary: PVDs keep a permanent drainage path even with considerable lateral displacement or buckling from soil movements.
sections.body: PVDs assure a permanent drainage path even with considerable lateral displacement or buckling under vertical or horizontal soil movements. (p. 2-10)
key_points: Drainage path survives lateral displacement or buckling

sections.title: Minimal Displacement
sections.summary: The small mandrel causes minimal displacement; its effect on disturbed-soil permeability can be designed for (longer consolidation time); no significant shear strength loss from remolding has been seen.
sections.body: The typical mandrel is small enough to cause minimal displacement during installation. The effect of displacement on the permeability of the disturbed soil can be taken into account in design, increasing the time needed for consolidation. There has been no evidence of significant reduction of in situ shear strength from remolding. (p. 2-10)

sections.title: Improved Quality Control
sections.summary: Quality control is simple: drain continuity is assured, so inspection mainly checks anchorage and depth.
sections.body: Quality control and assurance for PVD construction is quite simple. Because continuity is assured during installation, the major inspection duties are proper drain anchorage and proper depth. (p. 2-11)
key_points: Inspection: anchorage and depth

sections.title: Equipment Flexibility
sections.summary: Many types and sizes of equipment, static or vibratory, adaptable to minimal jetting; very light equipment for unstable ground.
sections.body: Many types and sizes of PVD installation equipment adapt easily to field conditions. PVDs are generally installed with static or vibratory force, normal equipment can be adapted for minimal jetting, and very lightweight equipment can be used on unstable ground. (p. 2-11)

sections.body: PVDs come in reels usually of 450 to 1,000 feet, each roll about 3.3 feet in diameter and 4 inches thick, easily stored. (p. 2-11)

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: For PVDs to accelerate settlement the subsoil must be moderately to highly compressible, low in permeability, fully saturated, loaded beyond its preconsolidation stress, not dominated by secondary consolidation, and of low-to-moderate strength; environmental and site conditions must then be checked.
sections.body: When PVDs accelerate settlement during loading, the subsoil must have moderate to high compressibility, low permeability, full saturation, final embankment loads exceeding the preconsolidation stress, secondary consolidation not a major concern, and low-to-moderate shear strength. If the soils meet these criteria, the project must still be evaluated for environmental and other site conditions (2.2.3.1 to 2.2.3.3). (p. 2-12)
key_points: Six subsoil criteria, including loads above the preconsolidation stress
Then check environmental and site conditions
sections.applicability: Checking whether PVDs are feasible.

sections.title: Geotechnical Criteria
sections.summary: Investigation must define the extent and depth of compressible soils and obtain high-quality undisturbed samples for consolidation and strength tests; closely spaced index tests locate strata, OCR with depth is needed, and piezocone soundings find thin granular layers (piezocone ch can be off by half an order of magnitude).
sections.body: The subsurface investigation must define the extent and depth of compressible soils and obtain high-quality undisturbed samples for consolidation and strength testing. Preliminary Atterberg limits, moisture and organic content at short depth intervals help identify strata and where to sample. Enough consolidation tests are needed to define OCR with depth, and shear tests for undrained and drained strengths. Piezocone (CPT) soundings identify thin interbedded granular layers that affect settlement-time extrapolation; piezocone dissipation tests could give field coefficients of consolidation, though ch from piezocone methods typically varies by half an order of magnitude from actual values (Bartlett et al. 2001). (p. 2-12)
key_points: High-quality undisturbed samples for consolidation and strength
Piezocone finds thin drainage layers; its ch may be off by half an order of magnitude
sections.applicability: Investigation needed to design PVDs.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: If the soils are contaminated, water draining through PVDs may need collection and treatment, and drains must not penetrate into an underlying highly permeable layer.
sections.body: If in situ soils are contaminated with hazardous waste, excess pore water draining through the PVDs may need to be collected and treated, and care must be taken that the PVDs do not penetrate a highly permeable layer below the compressible stratum. (p. 2-12)
key_points: Contaminated sites: collect and treat drain water; do not penetrate a permeable layer below
sections.applicability: Environmental checks for PVDs.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Site conditions affecting cost: uneven surfaces (benches at least 25 ft wide; slopes to 1 on 5 for shallow drains), headroom (drain depth about 10 ft less than headroom; segments cost up to five times), obstructions (pre-drill; N above 10 to 15 may need it), unstable surfaces, depths over 100 ft (crane; over 120 ft special masts), stiff layers, soft anchoring layers, access and utilities.
sections.body: Site topography and soils can strongly affect economics. Uneven working surface: PVDs cannot be installed economically on steep slopes, so benches at least 25 feet wide are generally needed; shallow drains can go in on slopes as steep as one on five, deeper ones need a level surface for uniform spacing. Limited headroom: drain depth should be about 10 feet less than available headroom; segmental installation (e.g., under a bridge) may cost as much as five times the normal price. Obstructions above the compressible layer (concrete, rock, rubble, slag, debris) usually need pre-drilling, as may dense layers with SPT N greater than 10 to 15. Unstable working surface: usually stabilized with geosynthetics and a 2 to 3 foot granular drainage layer, or timber mats or special lightweight equipment at higher cost. Extreme depth: PVDs have reached 200 feet; over 100 feet needs a crane and over 120 feet a very large crane and specialized masts. Stiff-to-very-stiff compressible layers needing full pre-augering: PVDs not normally advisable (disturbance; a sand-filled hole would itself drain). Extremely soft anchoring layer where drains stop short: anchoring is difficult, slowing production. Site accessibility and overhead or subsurface utilities (de-energize wires, angled drains, skipped widths) add cost. Consult experienced specialty contractors; all these cases have been overcome, but extra costs can be very significant. (pp. 2-13 to 2-15)
key_points: Benches at least 25 ft wide; shallow drains on slopes to 1 on 5
Drain depth about 10 ft less than headroom; segments up to 5 times the cost
Pre-drill obstructions and possibly layers with N above 10 to 15
Over 100 ft needs a crane; over 120 ft special masts; 200 ft achieved

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: PVDs have no structural function: they speed consolidation and strength gain, so where stability matters loading must be controlled (staged) or vacuum considered below 12 ft of fill. They accelerate only primary consolidation; typical depth limit 100 to 120 ft; well resistance governs only in rare deep, heavily loaded cases; not where full pre-drilling is needed.
sections.body: A PVD serves no structural function (except perhaps in liquefaction reduction): a shorter drainage path gives faster pore water release, settlement and strength gain, but initial strength is the same with or without PVDs. Where stability is a concern the loading rate must be controlled (staged construction) and monitored, or vacuum consolidation considered if the final or stage fill height is less than 12 feet. Without surcharge, PVDs accelerate only primary consolidation; secondary consolidation (particle reorientation under constant load, FHWA 2006) must be estimated and can be reduced by excess surcharge and/or longer waiting; high organic soils need careful evaluation. PVDs have reached 200 feet, but 100 to 120 feet is typical, with special equipment beyond 120 feet. Drain flow rarely limits consolidation, but for very deep drains with heavy loads and relatively permeable soil, well resistance may govern (Rixner et al. 1986a; Koerner 2012). PVDs are not recommended where all or the lower length must be pre-drilled; sand drains or other methods may be considered. (p. 2-15)
key_points: PVDs add no strength; control or stage loading where stability matters
Only primary consolidation is accelerated; secondary needs surcharge or time
Typical depth limit 100 to 120 ft
Not where the whole or lower length needs pre-drilling
sections.applicability: Limits on using PVDs.

sections.title: Alternate Solutions
sections.summary: Alternates: accept the time (or preload without drains, or accept post-construction repairs), bypass with deep foundations or a column supported embankment, reduce compressibility (stone columns, deep soil mixing, excavation and replacement), or reduce load with lightweight fill; combinations suit sites with stability problems.
sections.body: Alternate solutions fall into four categories: (1) accept time constraints without drains; (2) bypass the compressible soil with deep foundations; (3) reduce its compressibility by another ground modification method; (4) reduce the load with lightweight fill. With enough time PVDs are not needed, and a preload alone may suffice (compare its cost with PVDs plus preload); or excessive post-construction settlement can be accepted with repairs as maintenance. Deep foundations (bridge, or column supported embankment, Chapter 6) are effective but usually much more expensive and may limit future site use. Usually more expensive than PVDs: stone columns (accelerate and reduce settlement, add strength; geotextile encased columns for very soft soils, Chapter 5), deep soil mixing (Chapter 7), excavation and replacement, and lightweight fills (Chapter 3). Where stability is a problem, combinations may be warranted, e.g., stone columns or deep mixing in unstable areas and PVDs elsewhere. Lightweight fills do not improve soil but reduce settlement and stability problems. (pp. 2-16 to 2-17)
key_points: Four alternates: accept time, bypass, reduce compressibility, reduce load
Stone columns and deep mixing add strength; usually cost more than PVDs
Combinations suit sites with stability problems

sections.title: Prefabricated Vertical Drains
sections.summary: Installation methods (Table 2-2: static, vibratory, jetting, combinations) push a steel mandrel carrying the drain, anchor it, withdraw, cut and repeat like a sewing machine; mandrels about 5.5 by 2.4 in. diamond or 5 by 2 in. rectangular; anchors 0.5 in. cable or rebar about 8 in. long or sheet plates; splices overlap at least 6 in. with at least 10 staples; one or two laborers.
sections.body: Installation methods are listed in Table 2-2: static (chain driven*, sprocket driven*, cable pull-down*, heavy weight, hydraulic piston push), vibratory (offset hammer with fully supported mandrel*, direct hammer with offset mandrel*, inside mandrel with enlarged shoe), jetting (covered mandrel with outside jets, jet probe without mandrel) and combinations (static with vibratory*, static with jetting*, vibratory with jetting); * = currently used in the U.S. Nearly all use a steel mandrel protecting the drain, an anchor holding it as the mandrel is withdrawn, and reels threaded through the mandrel; they differ in how the mandrel is inserted. An installation mast holds reels, mandrel and drive, on a crawler excavator or crane carrier; specifications usually allow static, vibratory and/or static-vibratory (Figure 2-3). U.S. mandrels are diamond about 5.5 by 2.4 inches or rectangular about 5 by 2 inches, sometimes with a stabilizing fin. Anchors are 0.5 inch cable or rebar about 8 inches long, or thin sheet metal plates folding around the mandrel. The mandrel is driven to depth, withdrawn leaving the drain, the drain is cut with stickup and re-anchored, like a giant sewing machine; some masts are called 'drain stitches' (as printed). Very deep drains (150 feet) need large or special equipment; barges and marsh buggies have been used. Splices insert the old core into the new roll at least 6 inches, overlapping core and geotextile, with at least 10 staples (4 each side, 2 in the middle). Obstructions above the soft layer are pre-drilled or offset; those within it can only be offset. A one-to-two-person crew handles drains, cutoffs, rolls and anchors (Figures 2-4, 2-5). (pp. 2-18 to 2-23)

sections.title: Specialized Equipment
sections.summary: Specialized equipment may be needed for unstable or sloped surfaces, hard-to-penetrate subsoils and drains 150 ft or deeper (special carriers, marsh buggies, jetting skids, boring rigs for relief wells); obstruction pre-drilling should have its own pay item.
sections.body: Very specialized equipment is sometimes needed: unstable working surfaces, sloped surfaces, subsoils very difficult to penetrate, and extremely deep drains (150 feet or more). Examples are special carriers for deep drains, marsh buggies on unstable surfaces, external jetting on lightweight skids for steep slopes, and test boring equipment to install pipe drains with PVD material for relief wells in existing dams. Fills with rubble, concrete, old slabs or footings, buried riprap or boulders, and cemented layers may need special drilling. Pre-loosening by auger should be included in the PVD price, but where obstruction drilling is anticipated a special obstruction or pre-drilling pay item should be established. (p. 2-24)
key_points: Special equipment for unstable or sloped ground, hard soils, drains of 150 ft or more
Set a separate pay item for obstruction pre-drilling
sections.applicability: When specialized PVD equipment is needed.

sections.title: Staged Construction
sections.summary: On weak, compressible foundations, fill is placed in stages so the soil consolidates and gains strength between lifts, guided by settlement and pore pressure monitoring; PVDs shorten the waits between stages.
sections.body: Moderate to high embankments on soft, weak, compressible soils can settle excessively or fail if filled too fast or too high. Staged construction builds the fill in stages so the foundation consolidates and gains strength between additions; the rate depends on the soil's consolidation characteristics. Settlement and pore pressure monitoring shows when more fill can be added safely. It is used when time allows settlement during construction; PVDs speed consolidation and shorten the waits between fill placements. (p. 2-24)
key_points: Fill in stages so the soil gains strength between lifts
Monitoring decides when to add fill; PVDs shorten the waits
sections.applicability: Staged embankment construction with PVDs.

sections.title: Materials of Construction
sections.summary: Heading for materials: prefabricated vertical drains (2.3.2.1) and the drainage layer (2.3.2.2).
sections.body: Heading for the materials of construction: the prefabricated vertical drains (2.3.2.1) and the drainage layer that carries water away from them (2.3.2.2). (p. 2-25)
sections.applicability: Materials for PVD installations.

sections.title: Prefabricated Vertical Drains
sections.summary: A PVD is a channeled plastic core (flow path, shape, strength) in a geotextile filter; AOS of 0.15 to 0.074 mm (#100 to #200) has worked on all projects. Select by filter, strength, flexibility, durability, discharge capacity qw, resistance and equivalent diameter dw; assume a conservative maximum discharge capacity of 3,500 ft3/year. Smear from mandrel disturbance slows consolidation.
sections.body: PVDs are flat, about 4 inches wide by 1/8 to 3/8 inch thick: a plastic core forming channels and a loose geotextile cover, equally important. The core provides low-resistance flow channels, keeps the shape, supports the jacket and gives tensile and compressive strength. The geotextile keeps soil out of the channels while passing water and forms the outside of the channels. An AOS in the range 0.15-0.074 mm (U.S. #100 to #200) has been effective on all projects. Selection parameters: jacket permeability and characteristics, strength, flexibility, durability, discharge capacity (qw), drain resistance and equivalent diameter (dw). The filter should prevent passage or allow a natural filter cake, resist tearing and last through consolidation; discharge capacity under lateral stress, buckling and crimping matter (Rixner et al. 1986a; Chu et al. 2004; Koerner 2012). Assume a conservative maximum discharge capacity of 3,500 ft3/year. Opinions differ on small openings (against siltation) versus large ones (natural filter); Holtz and Christopher (1987) give criteria for critical/severe conditions (loss of life, major damage or repair cost above installation cost; gap graded soils, high, dynamic or reversing gradients) and for less critical ones. Disturbance depends on mandrel size and shape, soil macrofabric and procedure and slows consolidation; the smear zone it creates must be considered and is minimized by proper mandrel selection. (pp. 2-25 to 2-26)
key_points: Geotextile AOS 0.15 to 0.074 mm (#100 to #200)
Assume a conservative maximum discharge capacity of 3,500 ft3/year
Mandrel disturbance creates a smear zone that slows consolidation
sections.applicability: Selecting PVD materials.

sections.title: Drainage Layer
sections.summary: Water leaves through a granular drainage blanket or horizontal strip drains. Clean sand (under 3 to 4% passing #200) at least 1 ft, typically 1.5 to 3 ft (1 ft extra on soft soil or a geotextile separator; up to 3 ft where mud waves); clean gravel can be 8 in. between geotextiles; strip drains are about 1 in. thick, 0.5 or 1 ft wide, one per row (Figure 2-6). The layer must be outletted.
sections.body: The drainage layer conveys and discharges water from the drains, usually a granular drainage blanket; synthetic strip drains laid horizontally and connected to each PVD give a clear path without head loss, often outletted to gravel ditch drains at the embankment edge. A sand or gravel blanket can also be the working platform. Sand should be clean and washed, such as concrete sand with less than 3 to 4 percent passing the #200 sieve, at least 1 foot thick, typically 1.5 to 3 feet; directly over soft soils add at least 1 foot for contamination or use a geotextile separator (FHWA 2008); up to 3 feet has been used where mud waving is possible. Very clean gravel can be limited to 8 inches with geotextiles on both sides. Strip drains are about 1 inch thick and 0.5 or 1 foot wide, typically one per row of PVDs, occasionally one for up to three rows (Figure 2-6). The blanket may need thickening or geotextile/geogrid reinforcement to carry equipment; a combined platform and drainage layer is often cost effective. On uneven surfaces benching may break the blanket's continuity; the layer must be outletted. (pp. 2-26 to 2-28)
key_points: Clean sand < 3 to 4% fines, at least 1 ft (typically 1.5 to 3 ft)
Gravel may be 8 in. between geotextiles
Strip drains about 1 in. by 0.5 or 1 ft, one per row (Figure 2-6)
The drainage layer must be outletted
sections.applicability: Designing the drainage blanket or strip drains.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Part 4.0 (pp. 2-29 to 2-38): PVD design considerations and radial consolidation theory, the Rixner et al. (1986a) design procedure (Eqs. 2-1 to 2-3), preliminary spacing from liquid limit, and a design example.
sections.body: Heading of part 4.0, Design; it has no text of its own before 4.1. Its sections cover design considerations (2.4.1), the design procedure with Eqs. 2-1 to 2-3 (2.4.2), preliminary spacing design (2.4.3) and a design example (2.4.4). (p. 2-29)
sections.applicability: Core design equations for PVD drain spacing to achieve target consolidation within project schedule.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Preloading aims at a set settlement within a set time; PVDs shorten the drainage path. Design starts from Terzaghi settlement analyses without drains; radial drainage alone is usually considered since ch exceeds cv and the path is shorter. Barron (1948) radial theory, with triangular (Barron) or square (Kjellman) patterns and an equivalent cylinder (Figure 2-7), remains the basis.
sections.body: The principal objective of preloading, with or without drains, is a desired degree of settlement within a specified time; design uses fill or surcharge to preload and PVDs to shorten the drainage path (vacuum may also act as surcharge). Liquefaction applications need specialized knowledge beyond this summary (Rollins et al. 2004; Rollins and Strand 2007). Design needs the type, extent and properties of foundation soils and predictions of settlement amount and rate during and after construction and of stability in all phases. The investigation must define the compressible strata and obtain high quality samples for past maximum pressures, compressibility, and vertical and horizontal coefficients of consolidation; SPT N60 bears on installation cost and pre-drilling, and piezocone (PCPT or CPTu) is an excellent complement (FHWA 2002). Design begins with conventional settlement analyses (Terzaghi one-dimensional consolidation; Holtz et al. 2013; NAVFAC DM 7.1) of total and time rate without drains. Drains add radial drainage; although consolidation is two-dimensional, usually only horizontal consolidation is considered, since ch usually exceeds cv and the horizontal path is much shorter, reducing the problem to one-dimensional radial drainage. Barron (1948) gave the first radial solution in English for sand drains, still the basis of design, using Terzaghi's assumptions (homogeneous saturated soil, incompressible water and grains, one-directional flow and compression, Darcy's law, constant permeability and compressibility). Barron proposed a triangular pattern, Kjellman (1948) a square one; both use an equivalent soil cylinder of diameter dc with an impermeable outer surface and a central drain (Figure 2-7; Holtz et al. 1991). Solutions are in Barron (1948), Hansbo (1979, 1981, 2004), Rixner et al. (1986a), Holtz et al. (1991) and Han (2015); Rixner et al. (1986a) is used for the design procedure. (pp. 2-29 to 2-31)
key_points: Objective: a desired degree of settlement within a specified time
Usually only radial (horizontal) drainage is considered
Barron (1948) radial consolidation theory remains the basis
Figure 2-7: triangular and square patterns and the equivalent cylinder
figures: Figure 2-7: Drain patterns: triangular pattern (top left), square pattern (top right), equivalent cylinder (bottom).
sections.applicability: Theory and investigation behind PVD design.

sections.title: Design Procedure
sections.summary: Design selects PVD type, spacing and length for the required consolidation in the available time. Eq. 2-1 (Rixner et al. 1986a) gives time from dc, ch, F(n) (Eq. 2-2), Fs and Fr; dc = 1.05 x spacing (triangular) or 1.13 x (square); ch 1.2 to 1.5 cv, 2 to 4 with lenses, up to 10 for varved clays; dw = 2(a + b)/pi (Eq. 2-3), commonly 2.5 in.; Fs about 2 in sensitive plastic soils; Fr rarely matters.
sections.body: The design selects PVD type, spacing and length to reach the required degree of consolidation within a specified time. It begins with settlement analyses without PVDs; if 90 to 95 percent of settlement takes too long for the contract time, PVDs are used. Rixner et al. (1986a) relate time, drain diameter, spacing, ch and average degree of consolidation by Eq. 2-1, with the drain spacing factor F(n) from Eq. 2-2 (simplified); Eq. 2-1 ignores vertical drainage. t: time for the required degree of consolidation for a pattern, dc and dw; 90 to 95 percent is normally desired; vertical consolidation may be significant on major projects, often near 30 percent of measured settlement. dc: diameter of each PVD's cylinder of influence, 1.05 times the spacing for an equilateral triangular pattern and 1.13 times for a square one. To reach about 90 percent in 3 to 4 months, spacings are often 3 to 5 feet in homogeneous clays, 4 to 6 feet in silty clays and 5 to 6.5 feet in coarser soils. ch: laboratory values are fortunate to be within 50 percent; usually cv is measured and ch estimated: 1.2 to 1.5 cv with no or slight layering, 2 to 4 with discontinuous silt and sand lenses, up to 10 for varved clays with continuous permeable layers; layering is best assessed by PCPT; cv-liquid limit correlations (Figure 2-10) serve preliminary design. The best average ch comes from test fill or first-stage settlement data by the Asaoka (1978) method (Figure 2-8; Bartlett et al. 2001). Vertical drainage may be minor for layers over 15 feet thick and can be ignored in preliminary evaluations. With several layers, evaluate each; the lowest ch gives a very conservative spacing, but compute each layer's settlement. dw: Hansbo (1979) uses a cylinder of the same circumference, Eq. 2-3, with thickness a and width b (Figure 2-9); values of 1.5 to 5.5 inches have been used, 2.5 inches is most common, and 2.0 to 4.0 inches makes little difference. Fs, Fr: soil disturbance and well resistance are often ignored (Chu et al. 2004; Rixner et al. 1986a; Holtz et al. 1991). Under 'Considerations for Using Equation 2.1', sample disturbance is ignored except in highly plastic, sensitive soils with an accurately determined ch, where a 'sample disturbance factor' Fs of about 2 may be considered (as printed; Eq. 2-1 names Fs the soil disturbance factor); effects are greater at spacings under 5 feet and with large thick anchor plates. Well resistance is rarely significant except for very deep drains or high loads with very permeable soils (Hansbo 1979). Time, spacing and surcharge are the variables: more surcharge allows wider spacing for the same time (Fellenious and Altace 1999, as printed) or less time at the same spacing; usually time is fixed. Organic soils need extra surcharge to cover secondary compression within the available time. (pp. 2-31 to 2-36)
key_points: dc = 1.05 x spacing (triangular), 1.13 x spacing (square)
ch/cv: 1.2 to 1.5; 2 to 4 with lenses; up to 10 for varved clays
Eq. 2-3: dw = 2(a + b)/pi; 2.5 in. most common
Typical spacings for about 90% in 3 to 4 months: 3 to 5 ft in clays, 4 to 6 ft silty clays, 5 to 6.5 ft coarser soils
Fs about 2 only in highly plastic, sensitive soils; Fr rarely significant
Vertical drainage may be near 30% of settlement on major projects; ignore in preliminary work
equations: Eq. 2-1: t = (dc^2 / (8 ch)) [F(n) + Fs + Fr] ln[1 / (1 - Uh)]; time t to reach the average degree of consolidation by horizontal drainage Uh (U-bar sub h), dc = diameter of the drain influence cylinder, ch = coefficient of consolidation for horizontal drainage, F(n) = drain spacing factor, Fs = soil disturbance (smear zone) factor, Fr = well resistance factor (Rixner et al. 1986a); vertical drainage not included (p. 2-32)
Eq. 2-2: F(n) = ln(dc / dw) - 0.75 (simplified); drain spacing factor, dw = diameter of an equivalent circular drain (p. 2-32)
Eq. 2-3: dw = [2(a + b)] / pi; equivalent diameter of a band-shaped drain of thickness a and width b, a cylinder of the same circumference (Hansbo 1979) (p. 2-35)

Figure 2-9: Typical cross-section of a band-shaped drain and mandrel.

sections.title: Preliminary Spacing Design
sections.summary: Preliminary spacing from index data and geometry: estimate cv from liquid limit (Figure 2-10, NAVFAC 1982; center curve for virgin compression of good samples), take ch from piezocone dissipation if available (GEC 5), then solve Eq. 2-1 or use programs such as FoSSA for 90 to 95% consolidation in the available time.
sections.body: Preliminary PVD spacing can be set from soil index data such as liquid limit and project geometry (loaded area, depth of soft strata, need for surcharge). An approximate cv comes from liquid limit with Figure 2-10 (Department of the Navy 1982): the center curve is virgin compression of good quality undisturbed samples, the lower curve disturbed samples, the upper curve samples above the preconsolidation stress. GEC 5 gives more guidance on cv, and on direct determination of ch from piezocone dissipation tests. With the target primary consolidation set (90 to 95 percent), solve Eq. 2-1 or use vertical drain programs such as FoSSA (Adama Engineering 2003) for a spacing consistent with the available time; total quantities follow from the geometry. (pp. 2-36 to 2-38)
key_points: cv from liquid limit, Figure 2-10 (center curve for good undisturbed samples)
ch from piezocone dissipation tests (GEC 5)
Solve Eq. 2-1 or use a program for 90 to 95% consolidation
figures: Figure 2-10: Coefficient of consolidation versus liquid limit.
sections.applicability: Preliminary PVD spacing from index properties.

sections.title: Design Example
sections.summary: Example: 20 ft of normally consolidated clay with sand lenses over rock, 12 in. settlement, 90% in 10 years; target 90% in about a year without surcharge. LL 60 gives cv 0.1 ft2/day (Figure 2-10), ch = 2 cv, dw 2.5 in.: triangular spacing about 8 ft needs about 300 days, about 10 ft about 500 days. For preliminary design or checks only.
sections.body: A highway embankment over 20 feet of normally consolidated clay with sand lenses on rock: total settlement by one-dimensional drainage about 12 inches, 90 percent in 10 years (from classification data and a liquid limit of 60). With about 18 months available, PVDs should bring 90 percent within about one year without surcharge. From Figure 2-10 (center curve) cv is about 0.1 ft2/day; with horizontal sand lenses ch = 2 cv. Solving Eq. 2-1 with an equivalent drain diameter of 2.5 inches for 90 percent consolidation in a triangular pattern gives about 300 days at about 8 feet spacing or 500 days at about 10 feet. This feasibility method suits only preliminary design or a quick check of a detailed design, and the liquid limit must represent the compressible stratum. (p. 2-38)
key_points: LL 60: cv 0.1 ft2/day, ch = 2 cv, dw 2.5 in.
Triangular: about 300 days at 8 ft, 500 days at 10 ft for 90%
Only for preliminary design or quick checks
sections.applicability: Worked preliminary PVD spacing example.

sections.title: Construction Specifications and Construction Control
sections.summary: Part 5.0 (pp. 2-39 to 2-48): method specifications for PVDs, quality assurance in site preparation, materials, equipment and submittals, and instrumentation monitoring and construction control.
sections.body: Heading of part 5.0, Construction Specifications and Construction Control; it has no text of its own before 5.1. Its sections cover an introduction (2.5.1), specification development (2.5.2), quality assurance (2.5.3) and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (2.5.4). (p. 2-39)
sections.applicability: Specification requirements for PVD material, installation, and quality control in contract documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: PVD equipment, methods and materials are well established and design accuracy depends mostly on ch, so method specifications are almost always used.
sections.body: PVD construction equipment, methods and materials are well established with a proven record, design concepts are well understood, and design accuracy is almost directly tied to determining the horizontal coefficient of consolidation. Therefore method specifications are almost always used. (p. 2-39)
key_points: Method specifications are almost always used
sections.applicability: Specification approach for PVDs.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Agencies specify method and controls; the designer sets spacing, extent, length, drainage blanket and discharge drains; end result specifications are uncommon. Require trial drains, check drain sizes, and use the GeoTechTools guide specification or DFI (2014) Wick Drain Guide Specification, reviewing Hansbo (1986), Rixner et al. (1986a), Holtz and Christopher (1987) and Bo et al. (2005).
sections.body: Good specifications reduce problems, risks and cost and ensure the design objective. Agencies usually specify the construction method and controls; the designer details spacing, extent and length of drains, the drainage blanket (often under earthwork items) and horizontal discharge drains. End result specifications are uncommon, needing extensive exploration and design by the contractor. Specifications should give the installer flexibility, include QC and QA, and require initial trial drains to set procedures, checking mandrel size, depth gauges, splicing, verticality and materials. Inspectors should measure drain thickness and width against specifications and submittals, with laboratory tests if differences are significant. For GeoTechTools, eight state DOT specifications and the 2006 manual's guide specification were evaluated to produce the 'Standard Method Approach Specification for Prefabricated Vertical Drains and Fill Preloading'; another resource is the DFI (2014) Wick Drain Guide Specification (Method). Whichever is used, review Hansbo (1986), Rixner et al. (1986a), Holtz and Christopher (1987) and Bo et al. (2005). (pp. 2-39 to 2-40)
key_points: Designer sets spacing, extent, length, blanket and discharge drains
Require trial drains; check mandrel, depth gauges, splices, verticality, materials
Guide specifications: GeoTechTools and DFI (2014)
sections.applicability: Writing PVD specifications.

sections.title: Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Field control is simple: after trial drains, record each drain's depth and location, watch splices and rig verticality, sample materials, and note variances; inspectors must know the purpose of PVDs and report changes; also monitor blanket quality, fill placement and surcharge rate.
sections.body: A major advantage of PVDs is simple field control. After satisfactory trial drains, inspection mainly records depths and locations of each drain, observes splices and equipment verticality, takes occasional samples, and notes major procedural variances. Drains must be installed per plans and specifications, and inspectors should know the procedures and the ramifications of deviations, be familiar with drawings and specifications, and understand the purpose of PVDs; the engineer in charge should understand the whole solution (site preparation, fill placement). Inspection becomes repetitive, but changes should be discussed immediately with those familiar with the design. Drainage blanket quality, embankment placement and compaction, and surcharge loading rate must also be monitored. (p. 2-40)
key_points: Record depth and location of every drain; watch splices and verticality
Discuss any changes immediately with the designers
Also monitor blanket quality, fill placement and loading rate
sections.applicability: Inspecting PVD installation.

sections.title: Site Preparation
sections.summary: Site preparation (clearing, grading, working platform or blanket) must keep the blanket continuous; watch for mud waves or failure while placing it: over-thick mats have failed, e.g., a 5 ft haul road on a 2 ft blanket.
sections.body: Site preparation includes clearing, excavation or filling to grade, and building the working platform or drainage blanket, graded so the blanket stays continuous and surface drainage does not erode it. While building it, inspectors should watch for unusual soil movements indicating mud waving or potential failure. Mats or blankets placed too thick have caused very expensive failures; in one project a contractor's 5 foot haul road over a 2 foot drainage blanket, built for access before PVD installation, caused an extensive failure of the whole area. (pp. 2-40 to 2-41)
key_points: Keep the drainage blanket continuous
Over-thick working mats have caused failures (5 ft haul road on a 2 ft blanket)
sections.applicability: Inspecting site preparation for PVDs.

sections.title: Prefabricated Vertical Drain Material and Installation Equipment
sections.summary: Once equipment and materials comply, monitor verticality, depth and location; depths should vary only slightly between adjacent drains, checked against borings.
sections.body: Once equipment and materials comply, field observation is simple: verticality, depth and location. Local depth variations from the estimated depth are expected, but each drain's depth should differ only slightly from adjacent drains; the inspector checks pertinent borings to judge depth or a change in soil conditions. Sections 2.5.3.2.1 to 2.5.3.2.3 cover material, equipment and submittals. (p. 2-41)
key_points: Monitor verticality, depth and location
Depths should differ only slightly between adjacent drains
sections.applicability: Inspecting PVD materials and rigs.

sections.title: Material
sections.summary: Check the PVD material visually against the submitted and tested product: continuous core and jacket, correct dimensions, no handling or storage damage; many specified tests exceed what is needed.
sections.body: Before installation, the PVD material should be visually checked against that submitted and tested: continuous core and filter jacket, required dimensions, no handling or storage damage. Many specifications list intricate tests from manufacturer data that are often far beyond what is necessary, though a project may have stringent criteria. (p. 2-41)
key_points: Visual check against the submitted product
Many specified tests exceed what is necessary
sections.applicability: Inspecting PVD material.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: Check penetration method, mandrel shape, size and stiffness, anchor, depth and force measurement, and pre-drilling means; trial drains are recommended on all projects, witnessed by the owner.
sections.body: Inspectors confirm the equipment complies: penetration method; mandrel shape, size and stiffness; anchor type and size; method to measure penetration depth; method to measure and record installation force; means and procedures for pre-drilling. Trial drains to evaluate the equipment are recommended for all projects, with an owner's representative and inspectors present; variations needed to reach depth are evaluated then. Obstructions are usually offset, or predrilled or removed if extensive. (pp. 2-41 to 2-42)
key_points: Check mandrel, anchor, depth and force measurement, pre-drilling means
Trial drains recommended on all projects
sections.applicability: Inspecting PVD installation equipment.

sections.title: Submittals
sections.summary: Submittals: PVD type, specification sheet, source, installation method and sequence, rig details, mandrel, anchorage, procedure and splicing; often three successful projects of experience; do not require material delivery before the rig (two mobilizations); require manufacturer certification instead.
sections.body: Submittals include PVD type, specification sheet and source, and often an installation method and sequence. Installation submittals address rig size, type, weight, maximum pushing force, vibratory hammer rated energy and configuration; mandrel dimensions and length; anchorage; detailed installation procedure; and splicing method. Many specifications require a minimum of three successful projects by the contractor or its personnel. Specifications should not require PVD delivery before the installation equipment arrives, which would mean two mobilizations; manufacturer certification should be required in advance instead. (p. 2-42)
key_points: Installer experience: often three successful projects
Do not require material delivery before the rig arrives
sections.applicability: PVD submittals.

sections.title: Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Piezometers, settlement platforms and inclinometers monitor PVD performance and control fill rate; settlement data outrank piezometers when they disagree. Where stability matters, read daily and track displacement ratio DR (horizontal / settlement): about 0.4 is the upper limit for a stable drained foundation (Ladd 1991), 0.2 correlates with FS of 1.3 or more. Asaoka plots find end of primary.
sections.body: Instruments (piezometers, settlement platforms and gauges, inclinometers) monitor PVD performance and may control the rate of fill and surcharge; designers and instrument staff must understand each device and the strata. Settlement devices measure only rate and amount of consolidation; inclinometers measure horizontal deflection with depth and warn of instability; piezometers give consolidation rate and warn of excess pore pressure build-up. On many projects settlement rate has not matched pore pressure dissipation; then settlement data should be given priority. Simple projects without stability or time concerns need only surface settlement platforms; where stability is critical, pore pressures and horizontal deformations are needed, read daily during loading and for the first few weeks. Inclinometers go at the embankment toe or in front of walls, settlement plates and piezometers beyond the crest or near the centerline. The key stability tool is the displacement ratio DR, maximum cumulative horizontal displacement divided by cumulative settlement at an adjacent plate; significant increases signal a change from consolidation to excessive plastic deformation. Ladd (1991): with rapid filling DR approaching 0.4 may be measured, apparently the upper limit for a stable foundation with vertical drains; DR of 0.2 generally correlates with slope stability FS of 1.3 or greater; DR should decrease after filling (Figure 2-11, a multi-stage fill at the Woodrow Wilson Bridge Maryland abutment). Plot inclinometer data as cumulative and incremental displacement with depth and time (Figures 2-12, 2-13) to locate shear zones. End of primary consolidation comes from the Asaoka method (Figure 2-8; Bartlett et al. 2001). Install instruments after the drainage layer and PVDs to keep the site clear and place piezometers equidistant from drains, except that slope indicators and some piezometers and settlement devices should precede PVDs where stability is a major concern (typical layout Figure 2-14). (pp. 2-42 to 2-48)
key_points: Settlement data outrank piezometer data when they disagree
Displacement ratio DR = horizontal displacement / settlement
DR about 0.4 is the upper limit for a stable foundation (Ladd 1991); 0.2 ~ FS >= 1.3
Read daily where stability is a concern; Asaoka plots find end of primary

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Part 6.0 (pp. 2-49 to 2-51): the cost components of a PVD solution and typical unit prices by project size.
sections.body: Heading of part 6.0, Cost Data; it has no text of its own before 6.1. Its sections cover cost components (2.6.1) and typical project costs (2.6.2). (p. 2-49)
sections.applicability: Costs of PVD solutions.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: The unit cost of installed drains is only one cost; others are topography, obstructions and dense soils (N of 15 or more), installation methods (allow static, static vibro and vibro; jetting only with approval; no impact except pre-drilling), time, preload and surcharge, drainage blanket or strip drains, and design, instrumentation and monitoring.
sections.body: Cost estimates often consider only the unit cost of installed PVDs, not the total. Other factors: project size and topography (significant earthwork may be needed to level a site); obstructions and dense soils (very stiff layers, generally N of 15 or greater, boulders, old foundations, utilities raise cost significantly); installation methods (give the installer latitude; allowing static, static vibro and vibro is usually most economical; jetting only with the engineer's approval and no environmental impact; impact methods not allowed except pre-drilling through non-compressible soils); allowable construction and consolidation time (installation, fill, instrumentation, site preparation and blanket; usually the least variable factor); allowable post-construction settlement; preload and surcharge (type, material, reuse, amount; surcharge often limited by stability); drainage blanket versus strip drains (a granular blanket costs only its difference from local fill and may be needed as a platform; strip drains are a wholly added cost); design, instrumentation and monitoring (significant with staged construction); and the unit cost of installation. Time, surcharge and spacing are the significant variables to optimize: if time governs, spacing must close or surcharge increase. (pp. 2-49 to 2-50)
key_points: Installed unit cost is only one of many cost factors
Allow static, static vibro and vibro installation for economy
Time, surcharge and spacing are the variables to optimize
sections.applicability: What drives the total cost of a PVD solution.

sections.title: Summary of Typical Projects
sections.summary: Projects are small (up to 50,000 lf), medium (50,000 to 300,000) or large (over 300,000). Table 2-3: small $0.70 to $4.00, medium $0.50 to $1.00, large $0.30 to $0.50 per lineal foot, plus mobilization of $15,000 to $25,000 per rig, drainage blanket and instrumentation.
sections.body: Typical PVD costs fall in three categories: small, up to 50,000 lineal feet; medium, 50,000 to 300,000; large, more than 300,000. Table 2-3 gives unit price ranges for sites without major penetration difficulty, special equipment or unusual difficulty: small $0.70 to $4.00, medium $0.50 to $1.00, large $0.30 to $0.50 per lineal foot. A mobilization charge of $15,000 to $25,000 per rig is usually added, plus drainage blanket and instrumentation; unit costs can be much higher with severe weather, labor shortages, difficult sites or installation difficulties. (p. 2-51)
key_points: Mobilization $15,000 to $25,000 per rig

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: Part 7.0 (pp. 2-52 to 2-63): three PVD case histories: an interstate interchange reconstruction, approach ramps for a bridge replacement, and a substation site fill.
sections.body: The following three case histories illustrate successful projects: the Council Bluffs (IA) Interstate System Improvement Program (2.7.1), approach ramps for a bridge replacement (2.7.2), and the Jones Creek Substation site fill (2.7.3). (p. 2-52)
sections.applicability: Documented field performance demonstrating PVD effectiveness for accelerated consolidation of soft clay deposits.

sections.title: Council Bluffs (IA) Interstate System Improvement Program
sections.summary: Case history 1: PVDs with surcharge under interchange embankments on alluvial clays in the Missouri River floodplain.
sections.body: Heading for the first case history, PVDs and surcharge for interstate interchange embankments; its parts are the project description, subsurface conditions, design concerns, design, results and cost (2.7.1.1 to 2.7.1.6). (pp. 2-52 to 2-54)
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Description
sections.summary: A comprehensive redesign of about 18 miles of interstate; the I-29/US 275 interchange reconstruction (2014 to 2016) replaced bridges and embankments, raised grades and widened lanes.
sections.body: The Council Bluffs Interstate System Improvement Program modernized about 18 miles of interstate. The I-29/US 275/IA 92 interchange reconstruction (2014 to 2016) removed existing bridges and parts of embankments and built new embankments, a trail and bridges; six bridges were reconstructed, grades raised and lanes expanded, and railroad operations consolidated into a new corridor. (p. 2-52)
key_points: Interchange reconstruction with raised grades, 2014 to 2016
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Subsurface Conditions
sections.summary: Missouri River floodplain: about 15 ft of interbedded CL and CH (N60 4 to 10) over about 20 ft of CH (N 4 to 6), moisture about 40%, void ratio about 1.2, over silt and sand at about 35 ft.
sections.body: The site lies in the Missouri River valley floodplain: silty clay and sandy silt over medium dense fine to coarse sand. The upper 15 feet was interbedded lean (CL) and fat (CH) clay with N60 of 4 to 10; the lower silty clay, about 20 feet thick, was fat clay with N of 4 to 6; moisture contents about 40 percent and void ratios about 1.2. Silt with sand and poorly graded sand lay below, generally at about 35 feet. (p. 2-52)
key_points: About 35 ft of soft clay (N 4 to 10), w about 40%, e about 1.2
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Design Concerns
sections.summary: Settlement projections up to 30 in. under the added fill; removal and replacement was too costly and waiting too slow, so PVDs with surcharge were used in some areas and stiff columns in others.
sections.body: The alluvial soils raised settlement and stability concerns; added fill gave settlement projections up to 30 inches depending on fill height. Removal and replacement, surcharging, surcharging with PVDs, and stiff columns were studied; removal and replacement cost too much and waiting for settlement did not fit the schedule, so PVDs with surcharge in some areas and stiff columns in others were used. (p. 2-52)
key_points: Projected settlement up to 30 in.
PVDs with surcharge in some areas, stiff columns in others
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Maximum settlement 24 in. under about 40 ft of fill; 4 ft triangular spacing for 3 to 5 months after full height; depths to 35 ft; estimated 18,400 drains, 690,750 lf (Table 2-4); a test pad settled about 18 in. under 36 ft of fill, mostly in two months (Figure 2-15).
sections.body: Laboratory tests indicated a maximum total settlement of 24 inches under about 40 feet of fill. A 4 foot triangular spacing gave a settlement period of about 3 to 5 months after full height, with design depths up to 35 feet, in three areas: an estimated 18,400 PVDs and 690,750 linear feet (Table 2-4: area 3, 231,000 lf and 6,600 drains estimated, 129,494 lf and 5,850 installed in 9 days; area 2, 374,000 and 9,350 estimated, 234,192 and 8,111 installed in 13 days; area 8, 85,750 and 2,450 estimated, 74,391 and 2,367 installed in 4 days; total 438,077 lf and 16,328 drains in 26 days; source Menard Group USA). A test pad (Figure 2-15) settled about 18 inches under 36 feet of fill, mostly in the first two months. (p. 2-53)
key_points: Design: 24 in. under about 40 ft of fill; 4 ft triangular; depths to 35 ft
Table 2-4: 690,750 lf estimated, 438,077 lf installed
Test pad: about 18 in. under 36 ft of fill, mostly in two months
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Results
sections.summary: COLBONDDRAIN CX 1000 (4.0 by 1/8 in.) installed by chain or sprocket driven stitchers with a 5-1/2 by 3 in. rhombic mandrel in 26 days, average length about 27 ft; settlements of 4 to 20 in. were generally reached in 2 to 3 months, within the stated design time.
sections.body: The PVD was COLBONDDRAIN CX 1000, 4.0 inches wide and 1/8 inch thick, installed with an ALIMAK chain driven or APE sprocket driven stitcher using a 5-1/2 by 3 inch rhombic mandrel; the three areas took 26 days. The text calls the installed numbers and lengths 'slightly less' than estimated (Table 2-4 gives 438,077 of 690,750 lf, as printed); the average installed length was about 27 feet. Settlements of 4 to 20 inches were generally reached in 2 to 3 months, 'well within the design time of 6 months' (as printed; 2.7.1.4 gives 3 to 5 months). (p. 2-53)
key_points: 26 days to install; average length about 27 ft
Settlements 4 to 20 in. in 2 to 3 months

sections.title: Project Cost
sections.summary: Four bids from $476,465 to $823,396 for PVDs and fill embankments; PVDs about $0.50 per lf; mobilization for multiple rigs $40,000. Figure 2-15 shows test pad settlement versus fill height.
sections.body: There were four bids, from $476,465 to $823,396, covering PVD installation and the fill embankments. Subcontractor PVD prices were about $0.50 per lineal foot, and mobilization for multiple rigs was bid at $40,000. Figure 2-15 (courtesy CH2M-Hill) shows settlement versus fill height for the test pad. Acknowledgments: Iowa DOT, CH2M-Hill, Menard Group USA. (pp. 2-53 to 2-54)

sections.title: Approach Ramps for Bridge Replacement
sections.summary: Case history 2: PVDs for new approach embankments of a bridge replacement over railroads, including drains installed in segments under the existing bridge.
sections.body: Heading for the second case history, PVDs for approach embankments of a bridge replacement; its parts are 2.7.2.1 to 2.7.2.7. (pp. 2-54 to 2-59)
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Description
sections.summary: Replacement of a bridge over railroads with a new structure and embankments to newer standards; the west approach extends 300 ft beyond the old abutment, the alignment shifts about 70 ft north, and the old bridge stayed open.
sections.body: The project replaced the Tifft Street Bridge over railroads, between the Tifft Street-NY Route 5 ramps and Hopkins Street, with a new structure and embankments meeting newer standards (greater railroad clearance, wider lanes). The new structure was much shorter on the west, so the west approach extends 300 feet beyond the old abutment; the new centerline is about 70 feet north, and the existing bridge had to stay open until the new one carried two lanes. (p. 2-54)
key_points: West approach extends 300 ft beyond the old abutment
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Subsurface Conditions
sections.summary: 7 to 16 ft of cinder and slag fill over 2.5 ft of peat (west only), 33 to 46 ft of soft silty clay and 10 ft of sand on limestone; groundwater 1.5 to 3 ft deep.
sections.body: The profile was a 7 to 16 foot fill of cinders and slag over 2.5 feet of peat (west embankment only), 33 to 46 feet of soft silty clay, and 10 feet of sand on limestone bedrock; groundwater within 1.5 to 3 feet of the surface. (p. 2-55)
key_points: 33 to 46 ft of soft silty clay under slag fill
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Design Concerns
sections.summary: Embankments of 15 to 35 ft would settle 24 to 36 in. (west) and 12 to 24 in. (east) over about 6 years; PVDs were to cut this to 6 months, including drains to 55 ft under the bridge with 26 ft headroom and through slag with N over 100; 2H:1V slopes were stable only to 28 ft before strength gain.
sections.body: New approach embankments of 15 to 35 feet would settle 24 to 36 inches on the west and 12 to 24 inches on the east (much existing fill reused), over about 6 years after full height. PVDs on both approaches were to bring this within 6 months. On the west, part of the south side slope lay under the existing bridge, so PVDs to 55 feet had to be installed with only 26 feet of headroom to prevent future differential settlement. On the east, some PVDs had to penetrate 15 feet of abrasive slag under the existing embankment with N above 100 in places. 2H:1V slopes were safe only to 28 feet untreated; after PVD-accelerated strength gain the required 35 feet could be built. (p. 2-55)
key_points: Settlement 24 to 36 in. over 6 years without treatment
Drains to 55 ft with 26 ft headroom under the bridge
Strength gain let slopes reach 35 ft instead of 28 ft
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Settlement up to 36 in. west and 24 in. east; 36 in. surcharge; 4 ft triangular spacing where settlement and stability governed, 7 ft elsewhere; 229,600 lf of PVDs, 6,500 yd3 of blanket and 19,100 yd2 of geotextile, estimated over $800,000.
sections.body: The west embankment was expected to settle up to 36 inches and the east up to 24 inches. A 36 inch surcharge above final grade accelerated settlement. Spacing was 4 feet triangular where settlement was greatest and stability a concern, 7 feet elsewhere. The original estimate was 229,600 lineal feet of PVDs, plus 6,500 yd3 of granular blanket and 19,100 yd2 of geotextile; NYSDOT estimated the total over $800,000. (p. 2-56)
key_points: 36 in. surcharge; 4 ft or 7 ft triangular spacing
229,600 lf PVDs estimated
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Construction Procedure
sections.summary: Slag near the old embankment needed air rotary pre-drilling; about 82,000 ft went in on the east in 4 weeks; under the bridge a sectional mandrel (20 ft then 16 ft sections) reached 25 drains a day against over 300 elsewhere; some drains were angled under wires; about 110,000 ft on the west; more than one splice per drain under the bridge.
sections.body: On the east, special air rotary drills pre-drilled the slag near the existing embankment with the PVD rig following; farther away a combined vibro and static unit needed no pre-drilling; about 82,000 feet were done in 4 weeks. Under the bridge on the west, drains went in segments with a sectional mandrel pinned together (first section 20 feet, then 16 feet), through predrilled fill; after trials the maximum rate was 25 drains a day, against more than 300 elsewhere. The rest of the west side took 4 weeks, some drains angled under high tension wires; about 110,000 feet were installed on the west approach. Sectional installation needed more than one splice per drain, conflicting with the usual one-splice limit. (p. 2-56)
key_points: Sectional mandrel under the bridge: 25 drains per day vs over 300 elsewhere
Pre-drilling through slag; angled drains under wires
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Results
sections.summary: Maximum settlement 28 in. west and 24 in. east, reached in about 4 to 5 months, agreeing fairly well with predictions (Figures 2-16, 2-17 field data); slope indicators watched a marginal factor of safety.
sections.body: Typical piezometer and settlement data are in Figures 2-16 and 2-17. Maximum settlement was 28 inches on the west and 24 inches on the east, reached in about 4 to 5 months, agreeing fairly well with predictions. Piezometers, slope indicators and settlement plates tracked rate and amount; slope indicators were used because the factor of safety was marginal and to estimate the immediate settlement component from lateral movement. (p. 2-57)
key_points: Settlement 28 in. (west), 24 in. (east) in 4 to 5 months
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Costs
sections.summary: Several installation methods under one bid item: PVDs $2.10 per ft, blanket $17.00 per yd3, geotextile $1.40 per yd2; total under $600,000; NYSDOT then added a PVD mobilization bid item. Figures 2-16 and 2-17 give the field data.
sections.body: Several installation units (static with pre-drilling, static vibro, a special machine under the bridge) were bid under one item. Bid prices were PVDs $2.10 per foot, granular blanket $17.00 per cubic yard and geotextile $1.40 per square yard; on the original estimate the PVD solution came under $600,000, comparing well with projections. NYSDOT later added a PVD mobilization bid item for special equipment. Figures 2-16 and 2-17 give west and east approach field data. (pp. 2-57 to 2-59)
key_points: PVDs $2.10/ft; total under $600,000
A separate mobilization bid item was added afterward

Figure 2-17: Tifft Street east approach embankment field data.

sections.title: Jones Creek Substation Site Fill
sections.summary: Case history 3: PVDs, horizontal strip drains and surcharge under 18 ft of site fill for an electrical substation yard on soft fat clay.
sections.body: Heading for the third case history, a substation site fill with PVDs and strip drains; its parts are 2.7.3.1 to 2.7.3.6. (pp. 2-60 to 2-63)
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Description
sections.summary: Raising a site from elevation 5 ft to 23 ft for an electrical control yard above flood level, begun July 2015, with PVDs, horizontal strip drains, site fill and surcharge.
sections.body: In Freeport, Texas, the ground surface was raised from elevation 5 feet ('MLS', as printed) to 23 feet to put an electrical control yard above potential flood elevation. Work began in July 2015: clearing and grubbing, PVDs, horizontal strip drains, site fill and surcharge fill (final grading plan Figure 2-18). (p. 2-60)
key_points: Site raised from elevation 5 to 23 ft
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Subsurface Conditions
sections.summary: Gulf coastal plain: 2 ft of topsoil over 23 to 38 ft of soft to stiff fat clay (N 3 to 9, LL about 69, w 38%, fines 83 to 98%, e 0.95) over 10 to 15 ft of silty sand; groundwater about 5 ft deep.
sections.body: The site is in the gulf coastal plain (fluvial and deltaic sediments): about 2 feet of topsoil (loose sandy silt) over 23 to 38 feet of soft to stiff fat clay with sand (CH), over 10 to 15 feet of medium dense silty sand; groundwater about 5 feet deep. The clay was very soft to medium stiff (N 3 to 9), liquid limit about 69, moisture 38 percent, fines 83 to 98 percent, void ratio 0.95. (p. 2-60)
key_points: 23 to 38 ft of fat clay, LL about 69, N 3 to 9
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Design Concerns
sections.summary: 18 ft of fill would cause about 19 in. of settlement, only 25 to 50% within two years; sensitive equipment required PVDs and surcharge to slightly overconsolidate the soil; with no blanket material, strip drains each served two PVDs. Figure 2-18 is the grading plan.
sections.body: The 18 feet of site fill was estimated to cause 19 inches of total settlement at the center. From experience nearby, 10 to 20 percent would occur during grading (4 to 6 months) and 25 to 50 percent of consolidation within two years, too slow for the sensitive electrical equipment. PVDs shortened consolidation and surcharge put the soil slightly overconsolidated; lacking drainage blanket material, horizontal strip drains with two PVDs attached to each were designed. Figure 2-18 is the final grading plan. (pp. 2-60 to 2-61)
key_points: 19 in. settlement expected under 18 ft of fill
Strip drains instead of a blanket, two PVDs per strip
figures: Figure 2-18: Final grading plan for Jones Creek Substation fill project.
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: 4 ft triangular spacing for 90% consolidation in 4 months after fill and surcharge; average depth 35 ft plus 2 ft cut-off; Table 2-5: 12,468 drains at 37 ft, 461,316 lf estimated, 446,840 lf installed in 20 days.
sections.body: From three investigations and laboratory data, a 4 foot triangular spacing was chosen for 90 percent consolidation in 4 months after fill and surcharge. Design depth averaged 35 feet, with 2 feet of cut-off to attach to the strip drains. Table 2-5: area 1, 12,468 PVDs estimated at 37 feet including cut-offs, 461,316 linear feet estimated, 446,840 installed, 12,468 installed, 20 days. (p. 2-62)
key_points: 4 ft triangular for 90% in 4 months
Table 2-5: 461,316 lf estimated, 446,840 lf installed
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Results
sections.summary: MebraDrain 7407 (4.0 by 3/8 in.) installed with a hydraulic stitcher and 5 by 2 in. smooth rectangular mandrel by a three-person crew in 20 working days, average depth 33.8 ft; settlement 8 to 15.6 in. within 2 months against a 4 month allowance (Figure 2-19).
sections.body: The PVD was MebraDrain 7407, a polypropylene core with seamed geotextile, 4.0 inches wide and 3/8 inch thick, installed by a hydraulically driven stitcher with a 5 by 2 inch smooth rectangular mandrel to minimize disturbance; a three-person crew (two on vertical drains, one on strip drains) took 20 working days. Average installed depth was 33.8 feet against 35 estimated. Total settlement was 8 to 15.6 inches, generally within 2 months of fill and surcharge, inside the 4 month allowance (settlement plate data in Figure 2-19). (p. 2-62)
key_points: 20 working days, three-person crew
Settlement 8 to 15.6 in. within 2 months
sections.applicability: A PVD case history from the manual.

sections.title: Project Cost
sections.summary: Two bids; winning prices: $27,500 mobilization, PVDs about $0.45 per lf, strip drains about $1.50 per lf. Figure 2-19 plots settlement plate data and fill height versus time.
sections.body: There were two bids covering mobilization of one unit, vertical drains and horizontal strip drains. The winning subcontractor bid $27,500 mobilization, about $0.45 per linear foot of wick drain and about $1.50 per linear foot of strip drain. Figure 2-19 (courtesy Hayward Baker Inc.) shows settlement plate data and fill height versus project duration. (pp. 2-62 to 2-63)
key_points: Mobilization $27,500; PVDs about $0.45/lf; strip drains about $1.50/lf
figures: Figure 2-19: Settlement plate data and fill height versus project duration.
